findings.title: Spawn flusher workers are never killed or terminated
findings.body: Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, so they are SpawnProcess instances. SpawnProcess subclasses multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.Process (the default-context class). Both the hang-restart path (process.kill() around line 254) and join() (process.terminate() around line 346) are guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), which is always false for these workers, so the signal is never sent. Crash recovery still works because a dead process is simply replaced, but a hang does not: a second worker is started for the same shards, and once it updates the shared healthy_since value the slot looks healthy, so MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS never fires and the original worker is leaked. That leaked worker can keep calling flush_segments/produce on the same Redis shards as the replacement, duplicating buffered-segments output and racing flush state. On shutdown, a worker blocked in Redis or Kafka produce is also never force-stopped after stopped is set, so it can still produce after those shards have been reassigned.

findings.title: join() abandons flusher processes once the deadline has passed
findings.body: join() gives the entire caller timeout to next_step.join(timeout) before it waits on flusher workers. If that call consumes the timeout, deadline is already in the past and the loop breaks immediately, without waiting for or terminating any remaining flusher process. The previous single-process join always called terminate() even when the deadline had already elapsed. These workers are daemon processes only in the sense that they die if the parent exits; the consumer process stays alive across rebalance. A worker still inside flush_segments or Kafka produce therefore keeps flushing shards the new assignment no longer owns, which duplicates segments onto the buffered-segments topic and conflicts with whichever consumer now owns those Redis shards.

findings.title: Restart starts a new flusher before the old one has stopped
findings.body: _ensure_processes_alive replaces a worker by signalling it (when the isinstance check is fixed) and then immediately calling _create_process_for_shards for the same shard list. kill()/terminate() return as soon as the signal is sent; the old process is not joined, and its handle is overwritten in self.processes so a later join cannot reap or stop it. The old worker can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments while the new worker starts the same cycle. Both will publish the same segments and both will mutate the same Redis flush keys. The thread path used when produce_to_pipe is set never signals the old thread at all, so tests hit this overlap on every restart.

findings.title: Drift wait in test_basic is patched into a no-op
findings.body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op so the flusher thread does not pause, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to let that thread observe current_drift before join(). The test looks up time.sleep at call time, so it hits the patch and does not wait. join() then sets stopped immediately. The flusher can leave its loop before flush_segments runs with the advanced drift, so the assertion on the produced segment is racy. The new poll/sleep was added to close that race and does not. Nothing in the new test_flusher_processes_limit covers actual multi-process flushing, restart, or shutdown either, so the kill/terminate and overlap bugs above are untested.

findings.title: Flusher timers use mismatched, high-cardinality shard tags
findings.body: spans.buffer.flusher.produce is tagged with key "shard" while spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce on the next block is tagged with key "shards", so the two timings cannot be joined in dashboards. The value is a comma-separated list of every shard on that process, not one shard. The process-spans CLI defaults --flusher-processes to 1, which puts the entire partition assignment in a single tag. Each rebalance yields a new tag value (unbounded cardinality) and the string can exceed statsd tag-length limits, dropping the timings this change needs in order to tell whether the flusher is keeping up. The unhealthy counter already emits one bounded tag per shard and should be the pattern here.
